title: Faith and Science
lead: How Jews and Christians have read the Bible alongside the study of nature, from the rabbis and Augustine to Galileo and today. The main traditions agree that God's word and God's world cannot finally disagree; they differ over what to do when they seem to. The age of the earth and the days of Genesis 1 have their own page (The Days of Creation and the Age of the Earth).

sections.b:
The Bible praises God from both of his "books": "The heavens keep recounting God's glory" (Psalm 19:1), and "The LORD's law is flawless" (Psalm 19:7). The rabbis were ready to learn about nature from outsiders: when the sages of Israel and the sages of the nations disagreed about the sun's path at night, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi judged that the nations' sages were "more accurate than our statement," reasoning from springs that are warmer at night (Talmud, Pesachim 94b).

Augustine warned Christians not to make the Bible say foolish things about nature. In The Literal Meaning of Genesis (1.19.39) he wrote (own rendering of the Latin): even a non-Christian may know about the earth and sky, the movements of the stars, eclipses and the natures of animals and plants by sure reasoning or experience, and it is "very shameful and harmful" when he hears a Christian talking nonsense about these things as if from the Christian Scriptures; for if unbelievers catch Christians in errors about things they can test, how will they believe those books about the resurrection of the dead, the hope of eternal life and the kingdom of heaven? Calvin made a related point about Genesis 1: "Moses wrote in a popular style things which without instruction, all ordinary persons, endued with common sense, are able to understand," while astronomers study what lies deeper; their study "is not to be reprobated." Christian thinkers call this God's accommodation: speaking in terms people of the time could grasp.

When Galileo argued in the early 1600s that the earth moves around the sun, his opponents pointed to Bible passages that, taken literally, seemed to say the sun moves and the earth stands still (see The Sun Stands Still). In his Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615) Galileo replied that "two truths cannot contradict one another" and repeated a saying he had heard from a churchman of the highest rank, that the Holy Spirit means "to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how heaven goes." He was condemned in 1633.

The Catholic Church later revisited the case. Leo XIII taught in 1893 that "There can never, indeed, be any real discrepancy between the theologian and the physicist, as long as each confines himself within his own lines," and that the Bible's writers "described and dealt with things in more or less figurative language, or in terms which were commonly used at the time" (Providentissimus Deus 18). In 1992 John Paul II received the findings of a commission he had set up in 1981. He said (own rendering of the French) that most theologians of Galileo's day "did not see the formal distinction between Holy Scripture and its interpretation," that Galileo, "a sincere believer," saw this more clearly than his opponents, and that a "tragic mutual misunderstanding" had wrongly been taken as proof that faith and science are enemies. The Catechism (159) holds that research done honestly "can never conflict with the faith, because the things of the world and the things of faith derive from the same God."

Scripture as the measure of every claim. Many evangelical Protestants hold that the Bible is without error in what it says about history and nature as well as faith. The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978, Article XII) denies that the Bible's truth is limited to spiritual themes "exclusive of assertions in the fields of history and science," and denies "that scientific hypotheses about earth history may properly be used to overturn the teaching of Scripture on creation and the flood"; yet Article XIII allows for "observational descriptions of nature." Young-earth creationists go further: Answers in Genesis states that "No apparent, perceived, or claimed evidence in any field of study, including science, history, and chronology, can be valid if it contradicts the clear teaching of Scripture obtained by historical-grammatical interpretation."

Two books from one author. Catholic teaching (above) holds that when science and a reading of Scripture truly clash, the reading should be checked again, as happened with Galileo; Augustine and Calvin argued in the same direction. Some Christians accept the Bible's pictures of the world as God's accommodation to ancient hearers, as Paul Seely does (see The Firmament and the Shape of the World); others look for close agreement between the text and modern findings, an approach often called concordism. Jewish thinkers have taken a similar range of positions (see The Days of Creation and the Age of the Earth).

On this site the Bible is taken as true, and science as the study of the world God made. Where they seem to disagree, each view above is set out with its reasons, as on the pages linked here.
